extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers, mathematics instructors, and assessment designers interested in assessing students' proving ability
extracted.subtask_description: Developing or applying criteria to evaluate students' ability to understand (proof comprehension) and produce (proof construction) mathematical proofs; synthesizes literature-derived facets, common errors, methods/strategies, and assessment rubrics. Suitable for designing instruments or rubrics for undergraduate/secondary proof assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical proving ability (twofold composition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical proving ability is composed from two abilities: proof construction and proof comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper treats assessment of proving ability as derived from assessing both construction and comprehension; instruments should cover both domains rather than only one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof comprehension (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding a proof that has already been constructed: requires mathematical reasoning to determine relationships between premises and uses relevant knowledge to interpret omitted steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comprehension depends on logical reasoning (inference) and relevant background knowledge. Assessment models conceptualize multiple levels (surface to encapsulation) and multiple facets (e.g. basic knowledge, logical status, summarisation, generality, application).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehension level — Surface
rubrics_metrics.description: Surface level: students acquire basic knowledge regarding the meaning of statements and symbols in the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicator items: recognizing meanings of symbols and terms; operationalized in Yang & Lin's model as the first, lowest level of comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehension level — Recognising elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognising elements: students identify the logical status of statements used (premises, conclusions, applied properties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment looks for ability to label statements' roles within the proof; this corresponds to Yang & Lin's second level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehension level — Chaining elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Chaining the elements: students comprehend how statements are connected by identifying logical relations between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment targets understanding of inferential links and the flow of reasoning (Yang & Lin's third level).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehension level — Encapsulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Encapsulation: students interiorize the proof as a whole and can reflect on applying the proof to other contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highest level of comprehension (Yang & Lin): evidence includes recognizing what the proof validates (generality) and ability to transfer or apply the proposition elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yang & Lin facet — Basic knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Basic knowledge: understanding mathematical terms, images and symbols used in the proof; content of premise or conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational definitions include recognizing the meaning of a symbol, explaining meaning of a property, and recognizing directly applied conditions; used to build low-level assessment items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yang & Lin facet — Logical status
rubrics_metrics.description: Logical status: recognition of the status of premises and logical relations between premise and conclusion; judging logical order of statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalized as identifying whether a statement is premise/conclusion or applied property, and judging sequence order; groups with summarisation form mid-level comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yang & Lin facet — Summary / Integration
rubrics_metrics.description: Summary (integration): understanding the given, the claims, and the critical idea in a proof; identifying critical procedures, premises or conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment items ask students to identify the core idea or critical steps that derive the conclusion from premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yang & Lin facet — Generality
rubrics_metrics.description: Generality: recognizing the accuracy of the proposition/proof and what the proof actually validates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment looks for whether students can judge correctness and determine the precise scope or domain validated by the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yang & Lin facet — Application / Extension
rubrics_metrics.description: Application: knowing how to apply a proposition or proof in other situations; identifying premises applied in different contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tasks measure ability to transfer the proved result to novel problems or recognize when the proved statement is applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mejia-Ramos facet — Meaning of terms and statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure students' understanding of key terms and statements in the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple-choice items can target comprehension of vocabulary and individual statements; this addresses fine-grained, local understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mejia-Ramos facet — Logical status and proof framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the logical status of statements and the overall proof framework (which statement is being proven and the structure used).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Items probe recognition of which statements are assumptions, conclusions, and how the proof is organized (framework).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mejia-Ramos facet — Justification and claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure how each assertion in the proof follows from previous statements or assumed/known results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment asks students to identify or justify the inferential steps and dependencies between assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mejia-Ramos facet — Summarizing via high-level ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Students' grasp of the main idea of the proof and its overarching approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holistic items require students to state the central strategy or insight of the proof rather than local inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mejia-Ramos facet — Identifying modular structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the proof in terms of its main components/modules and the logical relationship between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment targets ability to decompose a proof into sub-proofs or modules and explain their interconnection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mejia-Ramos facet — Transferring to another context
rubrics_metrics.description: Adapt the ideas and procedures of the proof to solve other proving tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tasks ask students to apply methods or ideas from the target proof to new, related problems (transfer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mejia-Ramos facet — Illustrating with examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand the proof in terms of its relationship to specific examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Items ask students to relate the abstract proof to concrete examples or to use examples to illustrate the proof's scope/limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof construction (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructing a proof: creating an argument that attempts to prove a given theorem; involves examination of the problem, generating conjectures, selecting arguments, exploring content, and validating correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction requires relevant knowledge, the ability to generate and organize argument steps, selecting appropriate methods/strategies, and validating logical correctness. Assessment should consider whether the written proof answers the question and uses statements correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of appropriate proof methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Application of suitable construction methods such as direct proof, mathematical induction, proof by cases, contradiction, and contrapositive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choosing an appropriate method facilitates successful construction; misuse or inappropriate method selection increases difficulty and causes logical errors. Assessors should note method choice and its fit with the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof construction strategies — targeted vs shotgun
rubrics_metrics.description: Targeted strategy: develop deep understanding and plan before constructing; Shotgun strategy: try many plans quickly, abandoning on difficulty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targeted strategy is associated with higher success: plan based on understanding, possibly use graphical arguments, then formalize. Strategy choice can explain student approaches and errors; consider coding strategy use in assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student proof schemes (beliefs underlying construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students' underlying conviction for judging proofs: external/authoritarian, empirical (example-based), or deductive proof scheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deductive scheme aligns with mathematicians' standards and is the desired scheme; assessment and instruction can aim to move students from external/empirical schemes toward deductive reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common errors in proof construction (Stavrou classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent student errors: assuming the conclusion to prove the conclusion, proving general statements using specific examples, failing to prove both directions in biconditional statements, misusing definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These anti-patterns can be used as error categories in grading rubrics or diagnostic feedback; their presence indicates specific conceptual or methodological misunderstandings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment criterion — Logic (Moore)
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic: overall logical structure (proof framework), line-by-line reasoning, and correctness of algebraic manipulations and calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logic is the most important assessment aspect. Indicators: proof begins and ends correctly, steps follow logically, no invalid inferences or algebraic errors. Assessors often prioritize logical validity over presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment criterion — Clarity (Moore)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarity: explicit reasoning and justification of each step, coherent proof organization, and correct use of language and mathematical notation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarity includes stating reasons for steps, organizing the proof for readability, and using standard notation; clarity helps readers follow the logic and can be weighted significantly in assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment criterion — Fluency
rubrics_metrics.description: Fluency: use of language and correct mathematical notation (grammar and punctuation); errors here are usually given less weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While proper notation and readable prose matter, minor grammatical/notation slips are considered lower-weight issues compared to logical correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment criterion — Understanding (Moore)
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding: evidence that the student understands what they have written; a good proof shows the student's comprehension of the argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors look for signs the writer can explain or justify the steps in their own words; this may be measured via oral defense, commentary, or targeted questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof validation / assessor process (Weber)
rubrics_metrics.description: How mathematicians check a purported proof: (1) determine the structure of the argument and identify the proof technique; (2) if structure acceptable, check each line/step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validation proceeds from global structure to local verification. Note: there is evidence of inter-assessor disagreement and some subjectivity; standards may vary across mathematicians and over time, so rubrics should aim for clear objectivity but acknowledge variability.
